utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Today is Wednesday. Let me greet first the representatives of the OTP, Ms. Dahl and Mr. Mundis. Good afternoon, Mr. Seselj, and good afternoon, witness in Belgrade. I can see you on my screen. We are going to proceed with the cross-examination of the witness. Mr. Seselj, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stefanovic, we will now briefly deal with the method of financing, first of all, the Serbian Chetnik Movement, and later of the Serbian Radical Party. As you were then informed about all these party affairs, you ought to be aware that in 1990, I personally funded all the expenses of the Serbian Chetnik Movement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, if I may say something before this. The torture which I experienced yesterday before my testimony continued during the night and this morning. At about 2130 hours this evening, I wasn't at home, but my wife and my mother-in-law and father-in-law were at home. The police came to our door, or a para-police. I really don't know who sent them. But I've been living in that flat for years, and never have the police come to my door, except tonight. Allegedly, Borislav Nikolic sued me for offending His Honour or something like that. And my wife alarmed me this morning, told me not to come home. She said things were getting serious, as she's a lawyer by profession. I spent the night outside my home. However, the Republican Parliament, after two hours of debate -- or, rather, for two hours they debated about me, and then Tomislav Nikolic called upon the state organs of Serbia to allegedly investigate my property. They said that I had obtained my property by suspect means, that it should be confiscated. And he called upon the state to put an end to witnesses like me. This is now an orchestrated campaign against me, and in the course of today or in the next few days, the state prosecutor will probably react. Whether this is a directive that has come from The Hague or somewhere else, I don't know, but this is no longer a case of paranoia. The police came to my door at 2130 to arrest me, to bring me in. If the police don't know I'm testifying and that The Hague is superior to our judiciary, there's nothing for me to say. Another matter is the following: There was a verbal attack on me from the rostrum in the Assembly, and this was wholly inappropriate. And the state organs were called upon to investigate me. One can see that there is something that has been agreed behind the scenes. You can arrest me right now and take me wherever you like, but I feel much worse at present than the accused Seselj does, or anybody else, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, two things. I can do nothing with respect to the discussions that took place at the Parliament, but when it comes to what happened last night at 9.30 p.m., we are going to inquire with the relevant authorities about what happened. This is the first time I've heard about this. So to sum up, the Parliament members do whatever they like. We have nothing to say about this. But about the police coming to your door, we are going to try and find out what happened exactly and under what circumstances that took place. Mr. Seselj, please proceed with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stefanovic, you and I have been involved in the political life of Serbia for a long time, and I hope you're not surprised by anything that's happening to you now. Is this what you expected when, two years ago, you decided to stop being obedient to Djindjic and his heirs and refused to bear false testimony against me; did you expect to suffer unpleasantness?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's nothing to expect or not to expect. I'm telling you specifically, the moment when, through Judge Dilparic, I sent written confirmation to The Hague Tribunal in what capacity I wanted to appear before the Tribunal, the following things have happened. I'll give you a list now. In one night, my car, valued at 65.000 Euros, which was only five months old, went missing. It was taken away not by thieves or criminals, but I assume by state organs. I won't name them now. My car was stolen. My documentation, belonging to my company, was stolen, as was an expensive watch I had. And when I made a statement, the police did not oppose what I said, they were silent, and this confirmed that I was right. And then when the first subpoena arrived a month or a month and a half ago, that same moment the criminal police, dealing with economic crime, and the financial police arrived at my company, as well as some sort of state police and inspectors. Seventeen different inspections arrived. They dragged me out. They interrogated me. I could not devote myself to my business or to preparations for this testimony. When the second subpoena arrived, and I really don't know why subpoenas had to be sent to me, because I never tried to run away from this Tribunal, but quite simply the police arrived in my company and handed over to me this subpoena, and I was -- I'm only then expecting an avalanche, you who concealed this fact. This is now very serious, because my life is at stake and my family. What do I care about The Hague Tribunal and trials and so on? Yesterday, you kept silent about this. In 1994, there was a polemic between the UN and I, a tete-a-tete, and you can deny that. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, let me tell the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, let me stop you. You've just mentioned Mr. Nikolic, using totally inappropriate language about him. You can talk about his political views, but you can't go into any personal attacks against him. We are going to redact that part of your statement. Mr. Seselj, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I wanted to let Mr. Stefanovic know that I'm not willing to discuss this topic. But I absolutely disagree with your redacting the record, because Mr. Stefanovic is not speaking about what he measured, himself, but what was published in the newspapers and what was scandalous. So please do not redact the transcript, because that's been done too often in these proceedings. I'm truly not interested in this topic, and I don't want to discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stefanovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, the Trial Chamber has been extremely clear. Please refrain from any personal attacks about the behaviour or the sex life of anyone. You're not going here to settle accounts with Mr. Nikolic or whoever. You are not going to manipulate this Trial Chamber. And what happens in this courtroom is being broadcast in your country, so I'm going to be very clear. In your cross-examination, you are to focus only on what he said in his statements of 2003 and 2006, and you also have to focus on your responsibility in the charges levelled against you. The attacks against Mr. Nikolic and Mr. Vucic have nothing to do in these proceedings. Do not use this Tribunal to settle accounts in your own country. We are all aware that you held very high political positions. We know that you're a prominent political leader in your country. Please do not overstep the mark, and proceed with your cross-examination, focusing on everything related to the SRS during the years of 1991, 1992, or even 1993. That's what we are interested on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not clear to me in what way I'm dealing with Nikolic and Vucic through these proceedings and settling accounts with them. You are now holding this against me. I did not proof this witness. This is a witness of the Prosecution, not of the Defence. He should have been a Defence witness, and he himself wanted to be a Defence witness. He refused to be a Prosecution witness, and he was brought here under duress. But I did not proof this witness, and I, myself, am surprised by what the witness is saying now. And yet you're telling me that I am settling accounts with people. Yesterday, I prepared the questions I was going to put during cross-examination, which has nothing to do with what has been said now, so why are you holding this against me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness is not here under duress. He is here under order of the Trial Chamber to appear and give testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who said that the witness had been arrested? What is this an objection to? I don't understand this. Did I say the witness had been arrested? I didn't say that. Now, why this objection?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Seselj, please proceed with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stefanovic, it was clear to me in advance that you were going to have major problems, as do other witnesses who refuse to be Prosecution witnesses and ask to be Defence witnesses. I am not in a position to help you in solving these problems or to protect you from here, but what I know from my own experience is that the force of the public is the best protection against such problems. If you're able to, now please focus on my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj is giving advice and information to the witness, rather than asking questions pertinent to the indictment. I'd ask that his cross-examination be focused on the relevant issues and not directed at the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, please put your questions to the witness. You said earlier that you were going to put questions to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stefanovic, are you able to answer my specific questions? If not, I will give up my cross-examination right away.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look here. Even if I were in a much worse physical and psychological state than I am now, I would be able to answer your questions and the questions of the Court. But it's incredible that neither yesterday nor today have I been able to put together a sentence about the situation concerning my family, my property, my very life, but all this is being passed over as if the campaign against me is something that should not be interfered with. That campaign has been transferred to lower-level organs in Serbia, the Republican prosecutor, the police, or informal para-police groups or para-secret service groups. Well, not for a single moment have I been allowed to say anything, either yesterday or today. I'm being accused of being like this or like that. A woman came to my door unannounced when I was not at home. The police came in the middle of the night, when everybody was getting ready for bed, and I'm not allowed to talk about this. I'm not allowed to tell the reason why I left the party. It began with these staffing solutions, and they said, "Keep quiet. What are you talking about? Answer questions about silly things," about things I never said or signed. Yesterday, I analysed those signatures. They're not my signatures. They were scanned and only copied onto the Serbian language, because when I was signing, there was no translation into Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, yesterday you, yourself, confirmed that this was, indeed, your signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, please put questions to the witness to develop your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stefanovic, we are now talking about the method of funding first the Chetnik Movement and then the Serbian Radical Party in 1991 and 1992.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I asked you whether you were aware of the fact, in 1990, even before you and your party collectively joined the Serbian Chetnik Movement, that I personally funded all the activities of the Serbian Chetnik Movement?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And do you know how I came by the money I used to fund this movement?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the lectures that you held mostly in Australia and America.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You know that I gave 97 lectures in Canada, America, Australia, France, Germany, Switzerland and Great Britain in 1989, 97 lectures, and that two of my books were published abroad, one in Australia and one in Canada; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Part of that European tour I attended.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That was the second tour. We'll come to that.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm now speaking about the year 1989. Is that an indisputable fact?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: As we were on good terms and close in those years, you know that all the money I made, I didn't bring back to the homeland with me, that I left some of that money in Canada and America; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember there was a sum of about $100.000, maybe a little more, maybe a little less.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I will be precise. When interest was added, it came to $70.000 in a bank in New York, and this was blocked illegally when I came here to The Hague. $42.000 I withdrew from Canada in the early 2000s, and another sum, $15.000, from a bank in California I withdrew when I bought the house in Batajnica. You remember that the two of us together had a tour of Western Europe in January and February 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: We gave lectures to Serb migrant workers in Austria, Germany, Switzerland and France, and to Serbian emigres in Great Britain; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: We stayed there for longer than a month or a month and a half?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Forty-four days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And at these lectures, were tickets sold and were donations collected, and were newspapers -- was the newspaper 'Greater Serbia' sold, and were my books sold, and all this went into the party cash box?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you brought a large quantity of cockades which you sold, and this was your personal revenue, because you were unemployed at the time and had no income; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember what sum of money we collected when we came back to the homeland? If you can't remember, I seem to remember that it was 47.000 German marks, from different currencies, but that was the total in German marks. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I give it some thought, I think it was about 47 or 48.000 German marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was that the first money that we used to finance the Serbian Radical Party in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Immediately upon our arrival, it was set up, and you used that money for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: As the secretary-general, yourself, your basic duty was to collect financial resources for the Serbian Radical Party; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, in the Serbian Radical Party, did we pay strict attention to every dinar spent, every dinar coming in and every dinar coming out?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Since there weren't many of those dinars, we did pay strict attention to expenditure and incoming financial resources.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did we have two types of record-keeping; one was on the official account of the Serbian Radical Party and the Social Accounting Service, and the other was internal records within the party about the monies coming in?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and in the Social Accounting Service account, I had the right to sign for money to be withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you did this for the party; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, is it true and correct that we were very strict towards anybody who would try to embezzle even one dinar of party money?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember that Vojin Vuletic, for example, at the end of 1992, tried to appropriate 2.000 German marks belonging to the party and that he was uncovered in doing this by Secretary Ducic, and that he had to relinquish all his party posts and give up his work in the party?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was 2.200 German marks that an immigrant worker -- migrant worker had brought from Berlin. Dobric was his name, I think. And this was written into the book the secretary kept, and when Vojin embezzled this, he rubbed out the part -- the money trail. And when he was uncovered, he tendered his resignation, himself, I think, and then he went off and became a member of the Democratic Party. But soon afterwards, he became ill and then left again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And then Vojin Vuletic attacked us in the media when he left the party; do you remember all that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response].

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In the weekly magazine Knin, on television in some newspapers; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He moved and joined the Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember that my suggestions were that the attacks launched by Vojin Vuletic, that we should not react to them at all because I knew that he was, in fact, not a well man? So do you remember that we didn't launch counter attacks and didn't respond to those attacks of his, not by a single word?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that, that despite the attacks that he launched when Vojin Vuletic was hospitalised, when he went to the municipal hospital, that the two of us, and I think somebody else went with us, but, anyway, we went to visit him in hospital, after -- despite those attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Vojin Vuletic afterwards died, did he not?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in hospital, he was hospitalised, and, yes, he did die.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He suffered from a heart condition; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, do you remember, several years after that, my political adversaries, my political enemies, when they were angry with me, attacked me through the media and said that I had liquidated Vojin Vuletic; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I do remember that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yesterday, you were talking about the killing of Pasko Jovic, who is the wife of Slobodan Jovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, did we throw Slobodan Jovic out of the Serbian Radical Party already in 1993 and justified doubts that he was working for the Security Service of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Before he came to the Serbian Radical Party, he was an active member of the Serbian Security Service. He was sent abroad to carry out liquidations of our political enemies. And we did not know all this before he became a member, but when we did learn about his past, I think it was in 1993 -- maybe I'm wrong. Anyway, to be quite frank, he was a man who had a very negative past and was ready to do anything. He had very little education, although he did have some diploma or other saying that he had graduated from, I think, the Engineering Faculty, but in fact he was ready to take on anything. And later on -- I don't think you know this, but in 2000 -- or, rather, from 1999 to the year 2000, he showed his true colours, and I felt them on my very own skin. We were attending the party Saint's Day, and his party was the Nikolic Pasic Radical Party, I believe. Anyway, in the presence of my party colleagues, Miloje Mikisevicevic [phoen] and Mladen Bakic, in the presence of a large number of people from the very top positions of the DB Serbia, he said very ugly things about you. And then at one point, after having a brandy to drink, he started attacking me, too, and it was all I could do to escape that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, we'll have to cut that story short, the story about him. But what is interesting here and what it says in the alleged statement written by the Prosecution, which they say you signed, is -- refers to the killing of his wife. He had a very beautiful young wife, did he not, and she owned a bookstore somewhere in Rakovica; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, it was near my flat, and I explained that yesterday. After the statement, I conducted a detailed investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: We don't have to repeat that. We heard what you said yesterday. I remembered it all, so we needn't go into that again. But what I'm concerned about is this: Do you remember that for the first time, this man, Slobodan Jovic, for whom we know without doubt that he worked for the Security Service, during the silence prior to the elections, at the elections -- presidential elections in 1997, when I was a candidate who entered into the second circle, second round, that he published, in a daily paper called 'The Daily Telegraph,' on half a page, which was a violation of all the electoral laws, that I had killed his wife, and is that the first time he came out with that assertion?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, I would be lying if I said I knew exactly when that happened, but I know an article appeared in the 'Sunday Telegraph,' but I don't know -- or 'Nedelja Telegraph,' but I don't know but I don't know when that was, whether it was the pre-electoral campaign or the silence before the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. If you don't know for sure, we can move on. Now, Mr. Stefanovic, was I ever known as a greedy man; greedy, wealth, money, luxury living? Was that something that I was known for?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I always said how reticent you were and how you didn't like spending money, and in fact you preferred to take your meals at home rather than spend money in restaurants and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So what you're saying is that I led a modest life; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very modest. You wouldn't flaunt your money around. You were frugal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did I ever drive expensive cars or have any other luxuries, luxury items?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And is that how -- the spirit in which I led the party, too, that the party should be frugal, save money, keep a strict reign on money and just use it for actual party needs?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was there, yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, could anybody ever bribe me, a politician or some newfangled tycoon or anybody like that? Was I susceptible to bribery, was I greedy in any way?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and I can even quote examples. When somebody tried to do something like that, that they were publicly held to task.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And when Zoran Djindjic forced you to give your statement to The Hague investigators against me and to discredit me politically, then one of the forms of that political discreditation, pursuant to his suggestions, was to show me up to be as a greedy man who loved money more than his family and his party; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's like this: There's my statement. I went there contrary to my -- against my own will to give this statement to The Hague Tribunal. I don't know what was awaiting me there. I thought that they would hide things or -- I don't know. I resisted. This went on for two or three days, this resistance on my part, but they had focused on me so strongly that I had to give in. And the last conversation that I had, and I'm sure there's a witness of that, I was asked whether there was written trace of that, there's oral trace, because I went there with Mr. Batic, who at that time was the minister, and I asked for Mr. Batic's protection because I said I simply didn't want to appear in the Hague Tribunal, not because of Seselj, not because of who knows what, but because of me, personally, because if I did that, I would slam the doors to my political activity by doing that. It's what I live on. I have dealt in politics for 20 years. And he said, "Well, if Zoran promised you that you needn't appear, then why would you? And you know what the role of Carla Del Ponte was; not only the influence on the DOS, but on the 5th of October preparations and so on." And then as I was well aware of all those things, I agreed to talk to them. But this has turned into a never-ending set of games, and when I was thinking of this -- conducting this discrimination in the proper way, in a very correct way, then I had to use some political tricks. I had to resort to political ruse and say that the man was greedy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I would like to remind the witness that he is under oath and can be prosecuted for perjury.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you are under oath. You know better than anyone that you could be prosecuted for perjury. You know that, don't you? So are you telling the truth right now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please explain to me why the Prosecutor -- Madam Prosecutor doubts that I'm telling the truth. Why is that? Where does she feel that that has been the case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to explain to you why. I have before me a statement which you gave in 2003, and you repeated it in 2006. And in that statement, you said that Mr. Seselj was more interested in money than in politics. That's what you stated then.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And "more than his family," that's what it says there too.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, "family" too, I saw that, what you stated, and you added "or your family," but that's secondary. I'm interested in the money matter. And then Mr. Seselj asked you questions as to the financing of the SRS, and it seems that, based on his questions, the SRS was financed by the product of lectures he gave throughout the world. And you know that there are bank accounts abroad, into which the outcome of the lectures might have been transferred. So with regard to what you said in 2003 and 2006, there is an inconsistency with regard to your statement now, and the Prosecutor recalls you that if you were to say something that is not true, you can be prosecuted for perjury. You are under oath, so I'm asking you whether you are telling the truth now. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what I'm saying now, I'm saying under oath, and it's absolutely the truth. The statement given -- well, I wasn't under oath then, I hadn't taken the solemn declaration then when I wrote the statement. So please believe me when I say that this was geared towards discrediting Mr. Vojislav Seselj, so that statement was just given for those reasons exclusively. Now, I am under oath, I am telling the truth. We can look at the SD -- the accounts, we can go through the accounts and see where all these accounts are, all the cash inflow and expenditures, and things like that, the monies spent on television programmes, advertisements, pamphlets and so on. We have the SDK, Social Accounting Service, accounts, and we also have our own records in the notebooks that we kept. We can go through all that. And I am telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We know that you say you're telling the truth, Witness. Very well. Proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I think that we've dealt with the question of financing, then. I'd just like to focus on a number of details still. Do you remember that when the political parties in Serbia were being formed, that the pro-Western political parties were financed from abroad by different governmental and nongovernmental organisations; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not our party. Our party wasn't financed that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The Socialist Party and Kindred Parties, the League of Communist Movement for Yugoslavia and the Yugoslav Leftist Party, had at their disposal all these states institutions, did they not?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had firms within the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The Serbian Radical Party, did it ever have any large sponsor or financier who, for example, in the space of one year, provided it with a sum larger than 10.000 German marks, for instance, some financier or company or whatever? Can you quote any such example or any such case?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know full well how I collected money, that it was very arduous and it was difficult to make ends meet, and the expenditure was always greater than the money coming in. It was difficult. There was the financing of the Greater Serbia for posters. I gave 50.000 to Tijanic, for instance, when he was director of TV Politika, and then Studio B, Stojdinovic [phoen], just for one campaign, and that was in 1993; December, in fact. Or 1994, perhaps. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question for the witness, Mr. Seselj. At the time you were secretary-general of the Serbian Radical Party, does that mean that you could control its budget? Was that part of your remit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was like this: Not only did I have authority to control it, but I was the number-one man for collecting money, so I had to go around. I kept the treasury, I was in charge of the treasury, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. You're going to see why I'm raising this issue. Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Realtime translation continues] ... deposited at the Social Accounting Service. It was the only signature deposited there, which meant that I could withdraw money on the basis of that signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we heard a witness who was a member of the Serb Radical Party, and he said the following: I say this from memory, because I don't have the transcript before me, but this question just crossed my mind. But I know the case file inside out, so I can make a reference to it without having the transcript in front of me. That witness explained to us that it would happen that the SRS would send some of its men, volunteers, for them to guard plants, factories. He mentioned the guarding of a factory which gave rise to donations, sums of money, for the SRS. You were in charge of keeping accounts. You've just confirmed that. Do you have any memory, any recollection, of the SRS receiving monies from companies as part of surveillance activity by SRS volunteers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's a very good question, Mr. President. Bring that witness into the courtroom here so that he can face me. Who is this witness that says things like that, and who made him say things like that? That's all lies, and I say that with full responsibility. I have taken the solemn declaration here. I'm a Christian. I never lie. So, Your Honour, you are dealing with a man here who does not lie, who never lies. So that man was saying ludicrous things. He was telling untruths. And for as long as I've been a Radical, I've never accepted money from any companies. What companies, what guarding of factories, what's he all about? That's just not true. Bring him in here so that he can face me, and you can close the session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Stefanovic, that as the secretary-general of the Serbian Radical Party in those years, you travelled to Australia and spent a month there collecting donations for the party?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was there for about two and a half months.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, in my recollection, it was a month, but all right. Do you remember that you brought from Australia about 30.000 German marks?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's how much you managed to collect. Do you remember the largest amount you collected at one of your tours? This was during the pre-election campaign in 1993, when you came back from Berlin. Do you remember the sum you brought to the party treasury? What was the sum? I don't want to put leading questions to you. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know I gave all the money to Tijanic. I can't recall the precise amount, but I know I travelled from Berlin to Budapest by plane, and then as there were no planes flying to Belgrade, I came from Budapest to Belgrade by coach, and the election campaign was already on. I handed over the money. I can't remember the amount and the year. It's hard for me to remember those figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let me jog your memory. You brought 50.000 German marks back from Berlin, and we went to see Tijanic together. We went to Studio B, the television, and we went to 'Politika,' and we bought ads and we bought time, air time, for our broadcasts. And that was a time of huge inflation, comparable to that in Weimarkt Germany; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that the money I brought back did not cover those two television broadcasts. I know that we had to add more money to those 50.000 marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And do you remember how surprised they were in the 'Politika' TV when we brought various currencies; German marks, French francs, Swiss francs, Italian lira, Austrian shillings, Danish crowns, Swedish crowns. What else was there?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dutch guilders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And, yes, Greek drachmas. Do you remember that we brought along various currencies to pay for those TV broadcasts?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever was in the treasury, we brought along.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did we always go together when those payments were made and those contracts concluded?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I carried the money.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you were at that time the most reliable man for money.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- I was strong enough to carry the bag.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stefanovic. We won't talk about finances anymore. So that was the first form of my political discreditation on which Zoran Djindjic insisted. His aim was to eliminate me completely from the political life of Serbia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In 2001, I personally proposed, because they kept saying that the Serb Radical Party was upsetting democracy, the young democracy, the fledgling democracy in Serbia, and so on and so forth, I advocated the proposal that the state prosecutor ban the work of the Serbian Radical Party by a decree. And then a group of legal experts was established, which was supposed to draw up a text which would be sent to the prosecutor, and I think that this text was compiled referring to certain provisions of the Constitution and the various laws, I don't know what. And then they evaluated, and this was not something I wanted. I would have passed that law, but they said that it would be no good, that you would continue your work in other ways, that you would work underground, that you would continue your opposition work by other means. And someone from the top leadership of the state gave up this idea, and then they tried to eliminate you in other ways. There were some conversations which I heard with my own ears, where it was said that the Radical Party should not be interfered with, that it was sufficient to remove Seselj; that some foreign intelligence organisations were already influencing the Radical Party. And a year and a half or five years ago, I said that to some members of your party. I said that in 2003. There was an instructor called Steve or Steven, an American intelligence agent, who was brought by Zoran Korac to his flat, and before the elections for the mayor of Belgrade, they simulated a scenario. Zoran Korac pretended to be the television announcer, and this Steven, who was a drug addict and a homosexual and who was later found dead in a hotel, he pretended to be Bogdanovic. What was his name, Nenad Bogdanovic. And they did a role play, simulating the television broadcast that Vucic was supposed to have with Bogdanovic. I drew the attention of some people in the top party leadership to this, but they didn't pay much attention to it. Later on, foreign intelligence services exerted influence. When a group of the Serbian Radical Party went to Strasbourg, to the European Parliament, and then I had clear information as to who, when and was having meetings when they went to in Strasbourg. Foreign intelligence agents meant them there. Among them, Mr. Nikolic was recruited by a intelligence agency. So it wasn't just our own state security service that took part in Vukic and Nikolic's new political party. I was well informed. Mr. Seselj, you have not been in Serbia for several years, and you don't have the best information. Yesterday, I saw how wrong you were when you put forward the information about those three agents in Pristina. You don't know that America and Russia agreed to have their interest zones in the Balkans. Russia got Serbia; America got Kosovo. But some Jewish and Russian intelligence structures contacted Germany, and they want to expel America from its influence in Kosovo. They want Germany back there. You know that for a long time, there's been a love affair between Germany and Russia. It's been very intensive over the past few years.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Witness, we won't deal with geopolitical topics now, because my time is running out, and I doubt that this time the Chamber will extend my time. I would like to ask you to focus on more specific questions. When did you first learn that an indictment was being prepared against me in The Hague? You were one of the leaders of the DOS, you were in the very top leadership there, and you probably had this information.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the top political leadership in DOS, and there were many people there who were very inexperienced. They had never been in Parliament before, and I had good contacts with Zoran Djindjic, the prime minister, because his sister, Slavica, who was married in my village, the last name was Filipovic. And I visited his uncle Dusanic in Bosnia, and Ruzica, his wife, came from Valjevo. And you, yourself, know that in 1990, while Zoran was still wearing a ponytail and earring and jeans, that we were on good terms with him. For a long time, this went on. They rejected my idea which I still say would have been better had the Serbian Radical Party been banned in 2001, and the Socialist Party as well. They would have been eliminated from the political scene for a few years. But they took power and they, themselves, drowned in that power.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speakers are overlapping. It's impossible to interpret.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What year was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. This was quite some time before I went to The Hague. The indictment against me was brought in mid-February 2003, and I heard that on the 25th of January, 2003, that's when I heard about the indictment. Did you hear about it before I did, and how long before?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe I heard about it in 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. I have a newspaper text here. Could the Registrar please put it on the ELMO. I had it photocopied previously. I also had copies made for the Prosecution and the Chamber. This is a newspaper article I found last night when I got back to my prison cell, and it's from a newspaper published in Frankfurt called 'Vesti.' You're aware there's a newspaper called 'Vesti' published in Frankfurt?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the owner, Vidakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, that journal has been publishing a series, Tomislav Nikolic's confessions. And I got hold of this article which was published on the 21st of November, so let's see what Tomislav Nikolic said when Djindjic told him that an indictment was being prepared against me. Can this be put on the ELMO and can Mr. Stefanovic see this in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the text before me. Just telling if that's it: "The killer changed his mind." "The would-be killer changed his mind."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Dahl .

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: This document is not readily accessible to either the Prosecution or the Chamber because it is not in a working language. And I also question the relevance of the information -- that the witness can be asked questions and give answers regarding his knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, as to the relevance.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I ask that the original be given back to me so that I can use it. It's relevant because it refers to what the witness is now talking about. The witness is talking about the role of Zoran Djindjic, who tried to recruit him to be a Prosecution witness against me, whereas Tomislav Nikolic, in this article, says that Zoran Djindjic informed him that an indictment against me was being prepared. And I'll read the relevant part of the text to you now.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... test the witness's knowledge and understanding of facts relevant to the indictment. I object to Mr. Seselj reading a newspaper article to the witness, thereby giving the witness an opportunity to adopt information in a newspaper article. The point of cross-examination is to test the witness's own knowledge, not to feed him information to regurgitate.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I don't have the limitations that the Prosecution has in the examination-in-chief. I'm allowed to put leading questions. And I obtained this information only last night. You can check whether this issue of 'Vesti' was distributed to us last night. It was distributed in the prison yesterday, because it arrives with a delay. I saw this last night. I tore it out of the newspaper and brought it here. This is something very important for me. I could not have handed it over or disclosed it earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you know very well that this is not the first time this issue has been raised. The article is in Serbian, in Cyrillic. We're not familiar with that language, unfortunately. So you could very well ask your questions based on your reading of the article, but you are trying to know what the witness can say to your questions, but without him reading the article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. My fellow Judge has just said how you should go about it. Just say to the witness, "Here's an article. It was published in Germany on such-and-such a date, and the following was said in that article." You can sum it up very quickly, and thereafter you can ask your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have the right to quote a few articles from this article. I have no intention of reading the entire article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may quote a few sentences, but please try to be as short as possible. We don't want to spend too much time on an article which has not been translated for us. My fellow Judge has just mentioned it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it's impossible for you to have this in translation. That's a force majeure. I have marked the sentences I intend to quote. First, you see the paragraph before the last. Tomislav Nikolic says -- he says that he and Djindjic were in a specific sort of friendship and that they treated each other correctly, and that Djindjic, at the bar in the Republican Assembly, where they were having tea, said to him that an indictment against Seselj was being prepared. And he says that he told me that right away, but I know that's not correct. Tomislav Nikolic never told me that Djindjic had told him that an indictment against me was being prepared. Tomislav Nikolic confirms that he knew that an indictment against me was being prepared and that Zoran Djindjic told him about that personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What do you think about that, Mr. Stefanovic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Tomislav Nikolic is right. I think that either Cedo or Djindjic told him that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, first it was Cedo and then it was Djindjic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I know that they had a specific sort of relationship, a special relationship, and Nikolic -- what Nikolic says here, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Does that mean that Zoran Djindjic was already preparing the ground before I left for The Hague to take over the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I've already said in my testimony, the entire Radical Party did not have to be eliminated. They said that only Vojislav Seselj had to be eliminated. That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And then they could deal with the party easily; was that the idea?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And did you hear that recently Tomislav Nikolic accused me of having ordered his murder, commissioned his murder?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Tomislav Nikolic said something about Ruma.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And there was a big public outcry about what he said, and then some restrictions were put on my telephone calls here. And now Tomislav Nikolic is denying that. He says that he had a clear signal about a possible assassination, and that's in the second passage. And he says it was not prepared by Vojislav Seselj, "but he spoke so badly about me in The Hague, as did his associates, that I know more or less who could have said, 'Let's go and liquidate that traitor.'"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: This question has no relevance to the witness's fund of knowledge.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, originally Mr. Stefanovic's statement was compiled so as to depict my character in the blackest possible colours. I was the person who called Pasko Jovic, and then I had Vojin Vuletic killed, and the Prosecution has a witness they haven't called yet who will say that, and now Tomislav Nikolic says I ordered his murder. So I'm constantly commissioning assassinations, and no one can prove that I have any links to those. And here Tomislav Nikolic denies that it was I who commissioned his murder, and you here are convinced that I did. I could feel that in the courtroom here. And now I would like to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please ask your question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stefanovic, did I ever engage in any type of business?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except for politics, unless you -- is lecturing at university a business?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I didn't ask you whether I was employed. But was I a capitalist and engaged in any kind of business undertakings? That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The other way to discredit me, on the basis of what Zoran Djindjic said, was to link you up with Slobodan Milosevic and Jovica Stanisic as much as possible; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and the DB.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, and the State Security Service of Serbia. Well, in what the Prosecution has presented here as being your statement, it says that you allegedly said that I had excellent contacts with Slobodan Milosevic and the structures of the State Security Service, including Jovica Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hate to interrupt, but I wish to put on the record that Judge Lattanzi has left the courtroom and ask whether a break would be appropriate or if her absence will be extended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We may proceed without her. This is provided for by the Rules. Mr. Seselj, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Stefanovic, when I first met Slobodan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- if you want the time, the period, it was sometime in 1992, mid-1992, I think. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'll tell you in detail. We met briefly in the Republican Assembly sometime in April 1992, and we just became acquainted and shook hands. And then in May 1992, Slobodan Milosevic called me for the first time to come to his offices and to talk to him. Am I telling the truth?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that conversation was an official talk because it was with respect to the establishment of the federal Parliament. That's what it was linked to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It had to do with the first federal elections in Yugoslavia, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You should know, I think, that my political adversaries and enemies, the pro-Western media, on several occasions launched strong campaigns against me; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In those campaigns, did they use the worst possible lies and inventions, fabrications?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was it possible at all for me to respond to each of those newspaper articles or information put out on the radio or television about me? Was that feasible?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was impossible, even if you formed a team.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember that I collected all those worst attacks against me and published them in special collections of documents attached to my books? Do you remember I did that and that I was very fastidious in doing that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Katarina Ducic was in charge in the party with her daughter in collecting all these newspaper clippings and any footage in the media about you and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Zorica Zirovic was there, too, and a number of other party activists engaged in that. But not Zorica; Nada Zirovic. Do you remember her?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, fine. Now, I was accused of committing crimes, too, engaging in crimes?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And could anybody ever link me to any crime?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would say no, I had no knowledge or awareness that you engaged in any kind of criminal activity at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember that in 1990, I was in Milosevic's prison three times?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether you were just taken into custody or put into prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It was like this: In 1990, in September, for 15 days in Padinska Skela, because of my demonstrations in front of the National Assembly, then for 20 days because of a rally on Republic Square, then 25 days for another rally, a repeated rally. Do you remember that you came to visit me in prison in Padinska Skela at that time?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the end of those 25 days, you didn't want to leave the prison five days early, and they forced you to leave. You didn't want to be released. You took it to the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Our party wasn't registered, and while I was in prison, you personally organised a collection of signatures --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. Mr. Seselj, you raised a very relevant issue with respect to the indictment, and I would like to ask the witness to confirm that point for me. Witness, in the indictment, it is stated that Mr. Seselj took part in a joint criminal enterprise as of the 1st of August, 1991, until December -- or, rather, September 1993. Mr. Seselj asked you when he first met with Mr. Milosevic. I understand that you stated that it happened mid-1992. Could you be extremely specific and tell me when, to your knowledge, Mr. Seselj met with the late Slobodan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll be very precise in answering that. That first meeting, I know from what Seselj said. He said, "You know what? Today --" he was a deputy in the Parliament. Milosevic happened to be there for some reason. I wasn't a deputy, so I wasn't there, myself. But I remember him saying that he came and said -- we have a joke that we say "Pinky saw Tito," and he said, "Well, I saw Milosevic for the first time today." Seselj never went alone to see Milosevic. He was always accompanied by someone from the party, he always took someone from the party with him, so that whether it was one day earlier or later, but the elections were held in May 1992, and he contacted him with respect to an official meeting between the head of state and the head of a party. And I remember that on the 11th of June, I think it was, in the federal Assembly, that Slobodan Milosevic turned up and that the two of us were standing there together. Seselj and myself were standing together. Slobodan Milosevic came up to us, who had just entered the building, entered the hall, and he greeted him, and then for the first time with me, and said, "Good morning, Mr. Stefanovic." I didn't think he knew me, but he did know me. He knew my name and everything, and I was surprised by that. So that's what I know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, Witness. What you're saying is of great relevance. If I understand correctly, on the 11th of June, 1992, Mr. Milosevic came up to you, called you by your name and shook your hand. You were quite surprised. And he also shook the hand of Mr. Seselj. At the time, you were very close to Mr. Seselj. Can you tell us if, before that time, Mr. Seselj had already seen Mr. Milosevic, or was it the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He'd seen him before that. And according to what he told me, the story he told me, he came from the Republican Parliament, where he was the only deputy of the Serbian Radical Party. And he said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When exactly did he see him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know the date, but before that, several months before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Several months before. In any case, when Mr. Seselj testifies later, I'll ask the question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stefanovic, do you know when I met Jovica Stanisic for the first time?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I'll remind you. It was sometime in November 1992. There was a meeting of the Republican Parliament, and a deputy from the ruling Socialist Party came and said to me, "The head of the State Security Service, Jovica Stanisic, would like to have a meeting with you." I agreed, and he told me to go out in front of the Republican Parliament meeting and that Jovica Stanisic would come by in his own car. And that's what I did, I went outside. And several minutes later, a luxury car with dark windows drove up. The back door opened, I got in, and Jovica Stanisic shook hands with me. Did I tell you about that meeting of ours? And Jovica Stanisic on that occasion informed me that in Montenegro, an assassination against me was being prepared, whereas I had planned to go to Montenegro for the pre-electoral campaign. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't think you should go to Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And do you remember that I could not travel anyway because I had severe back pains, and I wasn't even able to stand on my own two feet during the election campaign, and on the election day I had a spine operation; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was Sunday, the 19th of December, 1992, in the morning. I went to the clinic where I operated discus hernia and I prepared -- or you did, and I prepared the elections in the party premises, and I wasn't able to go and visit you either that day or the next day because I was absolutely inundated with work. I remember that very well, and I remember the date very well, and the diagnosis, discus hernia. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I suppose it is. Now, do you know when I met Frenki Simatovic, Frenki, for the first time in my life?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I met him two years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I met him earlier on, and I'll disclose that secret to you. I met him in 2003, when Franko Simatovic, Frenki, was first brought to The Hague prison. That's when I first met him in my life. Do you believe me?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Frenki Simatovic told me that, too. Yes, I do believe you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, fine. Now, they ascribed to you that you had said the following: "I'm convinced, although I can't prove it, that Seselj was the executor of orders given by Milosevic." That is a sentence to be found in paragraph 20 of your alleged statement given in 2006. Did you indeed tell The Hague investigators that; is that what you actually said?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, nobody wanted to note down what I was saying about paragraph 21 and 26, but it's the same thing there. I never saw my statement, as I said yesterday. I asked at least ten times for the Tribunal to send me the statement in written form. I never received the statement, and it was -- I saw those pages for the first time yesterday, and these numbered paragraphs. I never gave a statement in the form of numbered paragraphs. That's quite unusual. So it's something that I cannot link to logic. And I just read points 21 and 26, 062436 is the document number, and that particular paragraph says that Frenki Simatovic did something. I don't remember what. But in paragraph 26, it says that your political advisers, or whoever, Professor Marjanovic and Mika Sprajc --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Just a moment. Do you deny having said this to The Hague Tribunal, that I was the executor of orders given by Milosevic? Let's take this one by one. Is that what you said? Do you deny it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I deny it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Stefanovic, at the elections in December 1992, the Serbian Radical Party became invigorated and we came -- became the second-strongest political party in Serbia; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 73 deputies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And the Republican government could not be formed without us; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you also remember that the two of us, you and I, went together to conduct negotiations with the leadership of the Socialist Party, to their headquarters in that skyscraper building at the Usce in Belgrade, the former Central Committee building?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Central Committee building, twelfth floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember that Milo Minic, Nikola Sainovic, and somebody else of the Socialists greeted us there?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was Bata Zivojinovic and Aleksandar Bercejg [phoen]. They were actors; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember that those functionaries of the Socialist Party offered us to form a coalition government with them, made that offer?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And do you remember that I persistently rejected any kind of coalition, but I said that we Radicals would agree to support a minority government on condition that that government pull the country out of the economic crisis and social poverty; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, afterwards, did we support the minority government, that is to say, the Socialist Party government?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And six months later, did we start toppling the government, since inflation had soared, poverty had soared, and the economic situation had, in fact, worsened?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After that, when we started toppling the government, there was a terrible attack by the Socialist Party or, rather, the parent authorities against the Radicals. They launched an all-out attack, and the papers buzzed with all this, and as did all the other information media, who had very negative comments to make about the Radicals. So there was an all-out campaign, an avalanche against us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, here again we are dealing with a point of paramount importance. We need, therefore, to be extremely precise and not to make any mistakes. You are challenging these statements that were taken in 2003 and 2006. You have explained to us why you challenge these statements. In this statement, it is stated that Slobodan Milosevic, together with Simatovic and Stanisic, controlled the Serbian Radical Party. That's written in black and white in this statement at paragraph 21 and at paragraph 20. And through the questions put to you, we find out that at some point in time, there was a meeting with the members of the Socialist Party with a view to establishing an alliance with that party. And in response to a question just put to you by Mr. Seselj, you've just stated that Mr. Seselj has refused any kind of alliance, and that's where we have a problem. If what is stated at paragraph 20 and 21 is true, we do not quite understand why Mr. Seselj would have been opposed to this alliance. If he was against such an idea during that meeting, then that means that what is stated at paragraph 20 and 21 is not true. Sir, can you confirm that you attended a meeting that took place with Mr. Seselj, yourself and members of the Socialist Party, with a view to creating an alliance, and that Mr. Seselj rejected that idea?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'll present two or three facts that can be borne out by people who are still alive and well and living in Belgrade today. I don't know whether Mr. Seselj remembers, but as a mark of goodwill, a gesture of goodwill, they prepared some cakes for us, some cream puffs. Well, there were no cream puffs or eclairs, so they brought some other type of cake I can't remember what it was called. Anyway, I remember something full well, and I don't think you know that today or knew it then, but when I went in to the other office, I was received by Zoran Andjelkovic, who was a high-ranking official of theirs at the time and today too, and we conducted a conversation in which he tried to persuade me to wield my influence on you to agree to form a coalition government and that he tried to recruit me by promising me a good position in that government, me and some others. And I said I did not wish to discuss the matter on my own or secretly. But I remember the conversation full well, and I remember you saying to Minic, since Minic was from my area and a school friend of mine, that if you cease to negotiate with them, that there'll be a much more radical stream who wouldn't want to give their support even to a minority government. So they agreed to your -- what you were offering him. So those are the details of that meeting. The meeting was held on the 12th in the former CK building, Central Committee building, with those eclairs and some Coca-Cola. And in addition to Minic, who was sitting there at the meeting, there was also Bercejg and Bata Zivojinovic, two actors. But Zoran Andjelkovic was sitting opposite them, and as I say, he conducted this conversation which you don't know about, which you've never heard about before today. He wanted -- he offered me a place in the government and said that we'd be given some important posts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you've provided a wealth of information with respect to the cakes and everything about this meeting, but what was the date of that meeting, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's difficult to answer that, Your Honour. You know what? I have a different approach to matters. I don't tend to remember dates, telephone numbers, people's names. I don't think that's important. So if you're asking about -- if there's a date concerned, I write it down in my notebook, I record it in some way. So I don't know years or dates, but it was about 10 to 15 days after the elections. That is to say, it would be logical that it was, if you worked it out and calculated it, it would be between the two Christmases, that is to say, the 7th or 10th or 15th of January, 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Stefanovic, after we tabled a request to topple -- overthrow the Socialist government, that the Socialist Party issued a proclamation that was published quite literally in all the media of Serbia and read out several times, in which they called me -- referred to me as a war criminal, a criminal, a madman and an alcoholic? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But they never managed to prove that I was a war criminal, did they?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I can talk about that. That had to do with attempts to have you come to The Hague and face the then Prosecutor. It was a woman. I'm not sure what her name was, Louise Arbour or something like that. And then through some embassies in Belgrade, because the Dutch wouldn't let you enter the country, they wouldn't give you a visa --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When the regime in Serbia accused me of war crimes, did I immediately express my willingness to go to The Hague, and did I ask for a Dutch visa so I could travel there; is that true?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's just what I'm talking about now, and the Netherlands refused to issue a visa to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Had they issued me with a visa, I would have arrived in The Hague in 1993, and I would have said, "Well, if you have something against me, here I am." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And did I say that for all the media?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'll tell you another detail. I don't know if I told you about it at the time, but I happened to be in the writers' club. I was having dinner with second secretary of the German embassy in Belgrade, Lilke [phoen], and I asked him whether Seselj could get a German visa, because you could use that visa to enter the Netherlands. And he said -- when a woman working in the Dutch embassy came along, I didn't know her, and this Lilke, who was the second secretary of the German embassy, said to her, "What sort of behaviour is that? You're not brave enough to issue Seselj with a visa so he can go and face the Tribunal, but we Germans are willing to issue him with a visa." I don't know what the woman answered. He didn't tell me the entire conversation, but that confirms what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a quarter to 4.00. We need to have a break now. One practical question. Tomorrow, we are going to be sitting in the morning at 8.30, instead of in the afternoon. The Registrar will take all the necessary steps for that. If needed, we may be working until 1.45 tomorrow, because we have two more witnesses to hear tomorrow. But now we're going to have a 20-minute break for the continuation of the cross-examination. Madam Registrar, please tell me how much time there is left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's just what I was going to ask. How much time do I have left? And another thing, Mr. President. Of course, I can always adapt to the time, but if the Registry can suggest that my transport be at a quarter to 8.00. If it's earlier than that, I have to ask the guards to unlock my cell earlier, because I need at least 45 minutes to get ready, to take a shower, to shave and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. The legal officer will make the necessary arrangements. Mr. Seselj, you've used one hour and ten minutes. You have 50 minutes left after the break. Let's have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Mr. Seselj, you have 50 minutes left. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stefanovic, there are two short questions I don't want to forget in connection with something we spoke about earlier. We mentioned cockades. You took those cockades when we went on tour and sold them. Did the Serb Radical Party ever manufacture its own Chetnik cockades or did we, like other citizens, buy these cockades on street stalls in the center of Belgrade and other towns?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Radical Party never manufactured its own cockades or any other insignia. I obtained them in Indija from a private manufacturer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Please tell me, you know who Nikola Kavaja is?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He died recently. He died recently. Why am I asking you this. I saw in some newspapers some photographs from his funeral. There was a guard of honour held by uniformed members of the Serbian guard of Vuk Draskovic. Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Members of the Serbian Guard, they wore black uniforms. Did you observe that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did the volunteers of the Serb Radical Party ever, ever, ever wear any kind of black uniforms? Did any volunteers of the Serb Radical Party ever wear black uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you sure?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
