utterances.text: Very well. We mentioned a little while ago this overthrow of the Socialist government and the communique issued by the Socialists against me and the Serb Radical Party. You're aware that Milosevic's regime arrested me on several other occasions as well?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let me jog your memory. In 1994, first they sentenced me to a month and then to another three months?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A total of four months in the central prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, because of the incident in the federal Assembly; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When Drasko Markovic, our federal deputy, threw water over the speaker of the Assembly, Radovan Bozovic, and the Assembly voted to expel him, and we did not allow the Assembly police to take him out of the room, and there was an incident, is that correct, and we wrestled with the police, literally?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I participated in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And then I was sentenced to four months in prison. I was the only one who served a prison sentence, is that correct, because I was the strongest? All right. And do you remember that a group of associates and I - you were not with us at the time - were arrested again in Gnjilan in June 1995 because we had organised a rally there which was banned by the regime, and we went to Gnjilan anyway?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You were in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. And then the police --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Intervened. They beat you up and took you to prison, and I came to visit you there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And I spent two months there in prison with my associates; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When Slobodan Milosevic was in power, did anyone ever attack Slobodan Milosevic and his wife, who was the director of the Yule [phoen] Direction, another ruling party, more fiercely than I did?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. I know that you even wrote several books about this. There was a large number of public appearances, appearances in the media, in newspapers, on TV. Let me remember -- let me try to remember the title of one of your books. "Mirjana Markovic was the Red Witch," and they were at Dedinje and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I gave all these books to the Prosecution a long time ago. The regime managed to arrest me only because of some incidents that had been provoked and that were quite innocent?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Had they had any information that I was involved in any sort of crime, or war crime, or anything of that nature, would not have they been eager to arrest me immediately and deal with me in that way at the time?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember when there was a reconciliation between the Serbian Radical Party and Milosevic and his party in 1998, and what was the occasion?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had already left then, but I think it was --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The situation in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the Kosovo crisis, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In your statement, it says here that "Milosevic gave me means and funds to implement the policies of the Milosevic regime." Did you ever tell that to The Hague investigators?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did Milosevic's regime ever help the Serbian Radical Party in any way, either with funds or infrastructure or in terms of organisation?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was a member, no. That I know for certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It says here in your alleged statement that I was often on the telephone with Radmilo Bogdanovic. Are you aware or do you remember that Radmilo Bogdanovic was a favourite functionary of the Socialist Party and that I -- he was the one whom I always liked best to attack from the rostrum in the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was on good terms with Radmilo Bogdanovic, and I continued being on good terms with him. And it's correct that for whatever reason, Radmilo Bogdanovic was often exposed to your criticism.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In paragraph 21, it says that the Serb Radical Party cooperated with Frenki Simatovic, the leader of the Red Berets. Is that correct, is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about this yesterday. It has nothing to do with common sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When there were fierce conflicts with the Milosevic regime, I often provoked Jovica Stanisic and Frenki Simatovic and so on, expecting them to respond in a nervous manner. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were quite a few attacks against the two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I would launch a provocation through the media and wait for their nervous reaction, thinking that then I could exploit it politically; was that what happened?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And I introduced a lot of confusion so that nobody could make head or tail of what was really going on?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was I a master in producing these propaganda effects?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never met a bigger master, someone more proficient than you in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You said, it says here, that we cooperated with members of the JNA General Staff; for example, with General Domazetovic. But you don't have precise data with how we cooperated with him, do you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether you know Domazetovic at all. I met Domazetovic only in 2002 or 2003. Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I met him late. He was already retired. But with my knowledge and my approval, Ljubisa Petkovic went to meetings with him to agree to the sending of volunteers. That's no secret. But you were not able to speak about this because you weren't involved or familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in contact with Ljubisa Petkovic at all, which is why, in my statement -- well, I say now he should have been sent to The Hague rather than you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ljubisa Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, he's already been in The Hague. He was sentenced, and he served his sentence.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that's what's going to happen to me, too, because the Prosecutor says the same thing that Tomislav Nikolic said at the rostrum. She's telling me that I'm not telling the truth. That's something that has been orchestrated, and all I can expect now is a prison sentence. Ljubisa Petkovic got off easy. He had a good time in The Hague for four months. He was assisted by Croats, Serbs, all sorts of people, and he got a place in Parliament as a deputy. And I will get a spanking. And it was said two hours ago that the state should take measures against those who are testifying in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stefanovic, the Prosecution cannot prove that you are lying. They cannot prove that you are lying, because everything you have said up to now in the cross-examination can be documented and it can be proved to be true.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you the truth quite sincerely. Yesterday and today, I've been speaking the truth, and nothing but the truth, and I've been speaking under oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well, very well.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that's propaganda.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I proceed, Your Honour? Have you intervened?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpreters can't hear me. The microphone is on now. There must be a problem, because I don't seem to be able to speak -- it's working now. Witness, you said something. It was a minor detail. It may have been a mistake in translation, but earlier on, you spoke about Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the interpreter cannot hear you. They are complaining to me, the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you turn off your microphone, Mr. Seselj. Witness, you mentioned a detail that was very quick, but I wondered whether there was a mistake or not. You said that Mr. Petkovic, he was convicted to a prison sentence, that he was assisted by Croats and Serbs, and that he -- he was now a deputy in Parliament. Is he now a deputy -- a member of Parliament?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think he is. Yes. I'm not sure, but I think he is, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which party is he a member of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Radical, the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: As you mentioned this, we'll have to clarify. Are you aware, Mr. Stefanovic, that Ljubisa Petkovic returned to the Serbian Radical Party some time ago?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He doesn't have to be on the party ticket to be a deputy. He participated in the election campaign, he participated in rallies of the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And he spoke at the rallies?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. And the party ticket was drawn up some two months before the elections; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It had to be, under the law, and he had to be on the ticket.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The elections were held in early May?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So in March, he had to be put on the party ticket; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the latest, maybe even before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And he was arrested in late May; is that correct? Do you remember when he was arrested?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was taken from the madhouse in late May.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Don't say that he was taken from the madhouse, from the asylum.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was kidnapped.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, he was in a hospital, in an asylum, not in a madhouse. Don't demonstrate your intolerance towards Mr. Petkovic in this way.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not demonstrating my intolerance. I'm just saying that he was kidnapped.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Any one of us, because of torture, various pressures and so on, can ask for the assistance of a psychiatrist; is that right? It's not immoral, it's not something to be sneered at, if someone in a difficult situation had to ask for help from a psychiatrist?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you misunderstood me, this whole story. In my public appearances and in newspaper articles, and still today, even 'Glas Javnosti' is writing about the torture of Serbian witnesses and the failure to punish other Siptar, Croat and Muslim criminals. So you misunderstood me. Please don't hold this against me, because I am trying to defend Ljubisa Petkovic, and I condemn what the Tribunal did. It's true that he was brought to the edge of reason, and it's quite normal that he should ask for help from a doctor. Every person has the right to get medical assistance when he's in difficulties. You didn't understand me properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Stefanovic, did you hear we had an eminent deputy, Dragan Tasic, who graduated in law in Montpellier in France, who was a very good lawyer, an excellent connoisseur of French and English, he spoke French and English very well, and he played an important role in the team assisting in my Defence? Have you heard of Dragan Tasic, he died?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know him personally, but I have heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Unfortunately he died at the age of 49 last summer, and when Ljubisa Petkovic returned from prison, the Central Homeland Administration decided that Ljubisa Petkovic should become a national deputy in place of the late Dragan Tasic. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the first time I've heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And as the Serbian Radical Party is a fierce opponent of The Hague Tribunal, the Central Homeland Administration felt that this was a way to honour Ljubisa Petkovic for his heroic deeds, because even at the cost of serving a prison sentence did he agree to testify for the Prosecution in the proceedings against me; is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I support what you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Stefanovic, just as I'm opposed to anyone showing intolerance towards you, I am also against anyone showing intolerance towards Ljubisa Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't trying to do that. You misunderstood me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on. Did the Serbian Radical Party ever, through its section, the Serbian Chetnik Movement, establish units in the interior of Serbia by municipality and local commune? Did we ever do this in the interior of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no need.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So when volunteers were sent to the front, they would first come to Belgrade, then go to the barracks in Bubanj Potok, where they would be issued with weapons and uniforms and sent to the front-line. And when they came back, each one went to his own home; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's just how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And here in this alleged statement of yours, on page 7, I see it says that -- they said: "Here I describe the hierarchy of the War Staff and the units on the ground which call themselves Chetniks." Did this exist in Serbia at all, a unit in Lapovo, for example, or in Gornji Milanovci or in Valjevo, where you were, and was there a commander of such a unit in Valjevo, for example? Did those ever exist?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what would those units be used for, what purpose would they serve? That's not true, there was no organised group of Chetniks on the territory of Serbia, because there was no need.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you this because we had a Prosecution witness here, whose testimony I challenged, who claimed that we had units in every municipality and that this military structure --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 2s and 3s?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, we won't go into this any further. Let's see what else we can clarify in what time we have left. There are some other things I have noted here. Mr. Stefanovic, in the course of the examination-in-chief, you spoke about something that is very significant to me. You said that you were recruited by the Tribunal to contact the Serbian Radical Party and, through the party, to offer me a trial in Belgrade, and that I would be released provisionally and given a sentence of only ten years, and that I refused this. Let's explain this in greater detail. First of all, who called you and who talked to you about this?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bruno Vekaric from the Tribunal. He said to me that he was asked from The Hague to try and contact the Radicals, and I told him I could. I had in mind that I could always come in contact with Dragan Todorovic, for instance, who was one of the men at the very top of the leadership in the Radical Party, and I did indeed come into contact with him. I rang him up on the phone, and we discussed it. I said -- in the Atos Pizzeria in Belgrade, and he came -- I said I was there, and he came several minutes later. And then we went up to the motorway so that we wouldn't be overheard by anyone, and I told him all this. And the story was as follows: That you should come and be tried in front of our own -- in our own courts, and that you would be given a prison sentence whereby you would be provisionally released immediately after the trial, and that would be the best possible solution for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you told Dragan Todorovic that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And Dragan Todorovic conveyed that to me, and I categorically refused with indignation; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the information, the feedback information I got from him. Dragan Todorovic rang me up, he said, "Let's meet," so we in the same place by the motorway; and that's what he told me. I didn't comment myself. I just listened to what he had to say, and he said no, he won't hear of it and so on and so forth, and then I told Bruno Vekaric the outcome, and some other people who were there when I told him, and then they all said out loud, "Well, heavens, he's a madman. Why doesn't he accept that? It's not a bad solution for him." And I said, "I don't know. I'm not his adviser, nor can I decide on his behalf. I did what you asked me to do as an intermediary." So I considered myself to be an intermediary of some sort, a go-between for the Tribunal, working for the Tribunal in one way in the morning and in another way in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And he was a spokesman of who, the Tribunal or the Special War Crimes Tribunal, he's a spokesman, isn't he, of the special prosecutor for war crimes, right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who were the other people present when you provided them with this feedback information?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember their names, although I could find out, because I know the people. They work in the OTP, but I don't know what their names are.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, I request that you demand Bruno Vekaric's written statement, the spokesman of the Tribunal in Belgrade, War Crimes Tribunal in Belgrade. I think that this is an important piece of information, and that he should be asked to state it all in writing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, can I ask you something? Did anybody, on behalf of Dragan Todorovic, ask you what I've just been talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dragan Todorovic told me about it personally, and I refused with indignation, because I never agreed to any bargaining or anything like that with relation to this trial, and I abhor anybody who entered into a plea agreement with the Prosecution. And I suppose that is common knowledge to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stefanovic, after my departure to The Hague, you took part in propaganda activities of the regime against me, personally, and against the Serbian Radical Party; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And during your stay here, you spoke against me, against my party and the Radicals, too, those Radicals?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Now, what influenced you? Was it my hunger strike that made you change your opinion and attitude straight away and then to offer yourself for my Defence team, to be a Defence witness?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, many things influenced me. It wasn't just one thing that was decisive. But when I saw that it was all a farce, after the incident we've just been talking about, about your being tried in Belgrade, et cetera, and many other things that seemed to me -- or, rather, many bad things that had happened to me, I was treated here as if I was a mentally-retarded child. I remember when the Prosecutor, the lady Prosecutor came, the one sitting opposite you, she said, "Good morning, Mr. Stefanovic." I said, "Good morning, madam." "Are you a Chetnik?" I said, "Yes, I am, I'm a Chetnik." And she said, "Well, you have honours -- honour and morals," and then I saw the aim of the question was different from what I thought it was, that people who were less educated say, "Yes, we Chetniks are special people, we don't lie and so on," so you can say something that should be said and should not. But my answer, the answer I gave her, was, "Madam Prosecutor, I am a politician, I deal in politics, and I can't be put in any category." And she was astonished and then we discussed this. Unfortunately, we haven't got the transcript of that or the recording of that conversation and what I said, but many circumstances and many things, especially when I saw the campaign launched by the whole of the West, and The Hague Tribunal as well, led by the OTP and the Prosecutor, for example, the state of Serbia is in a ghetto here, thanks to the Tribunal's insistence that we do something that they can't do. They can't capture Ratko Mladic, they can't capture Goran Hadzic, and unless we can capture him in the next ten years, we'll be punished. Who's going to punish us? The Prosecution and others will be punished for 100 years to come, and there will be no negotiation. They treat us like a banana state, a banana republic. So what I am experiencing today is something that I could never have envisaged. I don't think anybody -- I could never imagine that anybody would ever tell me to my face that I was lying, saying to a man that he's lying, who has never lied before.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly be asked to slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I understand that you are a politician, but this is not the place for you to launch, as you keep doing during this cross-examination, to launch into political statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, there is an important part --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the interpreters cannot hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that the microphone is not working. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, can you hear me? Witness, you just said something that might prove relevant. When Mr. Seselj asked you whether you had led a campaign against him, you said you did. But after that, it would appear that you decided to be a witness for him, and this is an important point. Was it you, yourself, who decided to tell the OTP and Mr. Seselj's Defence that you then felt that it was your duty to be a Defence witness, or were you forced to do so, to change your mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand the question, Mr. President, and I'll give you a very precise answer. When I gave my first statement here at the Tribunal, in these premises here, three floors above, I said quite resolutely to the investigators that this statement of mine can be used not only by the OTP, but that the Defence can use it, too. Now, the fact that they might not have recorded that is something that I did say. You can call the person that was there and heard it. So at that first interview, I told him that my statement could be used both by the Prosecution and by the Defence. So -- well, a witness is a witness. There's no Defence or Prosecution, as far as I understand it, in our system, at least, in my country. If you're a witness, you're a witness. Whether you're going to be a Prosecution or Defence witness or whatever, I don't know. But anyway, I was resolved at the time to be a Prosecution or a Defence witness, and then later on, who was going to exert pressure on me from the Radicals? They couldn't exert pressure on me for ten years, and now you expect Toma, who fled with the Americans, is he going to exert pressure on me? No, nobody can exert pressure on me. But quite simply, I thought it necessary to address the Tribunal in written form and state that in -- of sound mind, I am writing to the Tribunal to inform them of my intentions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The prime minister, Zoran Djindjic at the time, suggested that you talk to The Hague investigators about me. When that happened, did anybody -- was anybody present at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vladan Babic knew about this. It went on for two or three days, this persuasion, and then individually, too. And the final instance was that I was thrown out of his office, and I said I didn't know what to do. And quite frankly, at that point in time I didn't know whether I did or did not have to respond to the summons from the Prosecution, to be quite frank. If I knew that I didn't need to do that -- well, they kept saying that, "Well, you're a Radical and you don't want to help, you asked that the Radical Party be banned, you know them best," and things like that. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Vladan Batic was the Minister of Justice at the time, is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And he's still alive, luckily, so he could confirm your words?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Carla Del Ponte and Batic, they are both alive and can confirm that, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you personally have a meeting with Carla Del Ponte?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It was in the Cabinet, in Djindjic's offices. I knew that Djindjic was on good terms with Carla Del Ponte and that he said that he had managed to gain assurances that I needn't appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did Djindjic tell you what his motives were to send me to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I talked about that an hour ago, about the political scene, and that as far as you were concerned, all that was acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, this DOS, the Democratic Opposition of Serbia that came to power when Milosevic was overthrown; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, at the head of this party of yours, the DOS, did they feel that you would take over the whole party, the control of the whole party if I were to leave?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Cedo was in charge of that on behalf of the DOS. I dealt with the Socialists more, and I managed to fulfill my assignment and to split the Socialist Party into two streams. If you remember that time, Baki and Bani and Ivkovic and so on, so I was in charge of dealing with the Socialist Party of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You mean Cedomir Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Cedomir Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly be asked to slow down for the benefit of everyone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In paragraph 26 of your statement, it says the following: That the Serbian Radical Party had its intelligence organs and that you knew two men who worked as military intelligence organs. And to be quite true, I was astounded when I read here that you named Professor Jovan Marjanovic from the Faculty of Political Sciences, and also Colonel General Bozidar Stevanovic, also known as Mika Sprajc. Now, why was I astonished to hear that? Because you, Mr. Stefanovic, knew full well that within the frameworks of the political alliance, we really did have a group of retired military officers who dealt in intelligence. Do you remember that we had that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, but I don't remember that these two men were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, do you remember who was there? Let me remind you. Do you remember Colonel Milos Dimitrijevic, for instance, whom we called Stojan in order to cover up his presence? Do you remember Stojan?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he's a good friend of mine today, and we're still in contact. I remember Miso Dimitrijevic very well, and in 2002 or '3 he shared an office with me in Nemanjema [phoen] Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember that he would bring to my office every morning intelligence reports on the events on the political scene that happened the previous day?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and he did all that while you were in prison in 1994. And then he came to see me one morning, and I sent him packing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Something else happened, Mr. Stefanovic. We'll come to that in due course. I'm sure I'll jog your memory. But do you remember the captain of the naval ship Rade Suljagic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was he one of the people who provided me with very important information as well and who, in a way, was an adviser, too, in certain areas?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Not every day, but Colonel Milos Dimitrijevic did, not to mention other people, because the general public doesn't know them. But, anyway, do you remember, when I was arrested in 1994, that recently afterwards, Colonel Dimitrijevic was arrested too?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And do you remember that he was remanded in custody by the State Security Service for several days?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wasn't officially arrested. He was kidnapped.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember that four months later, upon leaving prison, I broke up that party organ of ours, I disbanded it, because I considered that the State Security Service was controlling it and that I was on the lookout for new people who would work for the party leadership and deal with those affairs; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember discussions about that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, do you also remember that not until the present day, nobody has managed to learn who those people are and who is the person behind the name Laufer, whether it's just one person or more people; are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you should know that I published a number of books. Laufer has contacted me, Laufer hasn't forgotten me, a Chetnik head over the Osmanli [phoen] whatever. Do you remember that the newspapers wrote about that in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A journalist told me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And they haven't managed to learn who those intelligence men were to this day, those people who provide me with reliable intelligence in various areas. Not even Tomislav Nikolic knows that, knows their identity; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He said Jadranko Vukovic was allegedly a go-between between myself and those intelligence men, but he never learned who those men -- those informers were, either. So I've learned something when it comes to intelligence work, have I not? Am I right? How much more time have I got, Judges?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I was wondering also, how much time you had left. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the Registrar, you have 25 minutes left. I found it rather surprising, but, yes, you have 25 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I might not use all the 25 minutes, but I'll do my best to use them all up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yesterday, in response to a question from Judge Harhoff, you seemed a bit disoriented. He asked you about the transport of the bodies of killed members or volunteers of the Radical Party. And I decided that this was because -- that your confusion came from --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the rest.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The problem is that the War Staff -- now, when I looked at the recording again and transferred it again, and I'll let the Trial Chamber be the judges, I couldn't remember that it was the Crisis Staff before, that that's what it was called before. And now in talking to people this morning, it became clear to me. So when the question of coffins was brought up, and whatever else, that was something -- well, if they'd asked me about surgery, I might have known more. So I'm not the right person to answer that kind of question. But the man asked me, so I had to answer. So it wasn't that I was confused; it was that I didn't know what to -- what answer to give. And, quite frankly, I do know that some people were killed over there, but what happened, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I would like to remind you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: You have to observe a pause between question and answer. Your last question, for instance, Mr. Seselj, was never translated. I didn't know what you were asking. So please make sure that you make a break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm referring to your questions of last night, Mr. Harhoff. I wish to remind Mr. Stefanovic that all the work about transferring the bodies of volunteers who had been killed to Serbia was performed by the appropriate service of the JNA. They used their medical vehicles and their helicopters to transport the bodies. All the funerals were paid for by the state. And starting from September 1991 onwards, a platoon of the army from the local garrison would fire a salvo every time there was a military band playing at the funeral. And officials of our party were always present. I was often present, personally. We made speeches.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember that, Mr. Stefanovic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never participated in any of the funerals. I assume all this is true. It's all very logical. These people were incorporated into the units of the JNA, as it was -- or whatever it was called then. But I was confused by this insistence that we should do something that I was not informed about. I don't know how they were transferred, how the coffins were transported. It's logical that the army did that. It's true that there was always a military band playing. It's true that a volunteer who was killed was always buried with all the honours due to a soldier of the JNA and of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And do you remember that volunteers who were wounded were treated at the Military Academy Hospital in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were treated just like every soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And is years of service counted for every member of the Serbian Radical Party who was a volunteer, and that those who became invalids were given a pension and all the benefits they were entitled to?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were always treated as regular soldiers of the Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. Judge Harhoff asked you how the exchange of prisoners took place. Are you aware that a certain number of volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party were taken prisoner by the Croats in the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware, for example, that 11 volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party, in December 1991, were killed defending Masicka Sargovina in Western Slavonia, and that some were wounded or taken prisoner?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Dragan Jovanovic, a friend of mine, was killed there, and Sigma [phoen] and Ducica [phoen] were taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It wasn't Dragan Jovanovic, it was Dragan Lazarevic, sir.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you're right, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He was a common friend of ours and a member of the party leadership?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I made an error.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And he was killed there. He was an only son; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember who conducted the negotiations concerning their exchange? They were arrested, put into a Croatian prison in Gradiska, I think. They are tortured in prison. And who was in charge of negotiations concerning their exchange; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I was in Australia at the time, so I don't know the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I'll tell you that the JNA was in charge of all the negotiations concerning exchanges, and we kept telephoning and trying to get the structure in the General Staff to get the exchange performed as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was present on several occasions when you personally telephoned the chief of the General Staff concerning some other exchanges; saving someone, I don't know. But it was always the army that was called up -- that was contacted on the telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it correct that all the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party taken prisoner by the Croats were ultimately exchanged and that not a single one was ever accused by the Croatian authorities of having committed a war crime; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it correct that not a single volunteer of the Serbian Radical Party who went from Serbia to fight for the Serbian Krajina or for Republika Srpska was ever accused of a specific war crime by the Croat or Muslim authorities?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, they had no reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you confirm what I say in my question?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Explain one other thing to me. Although you personally did not work on this, but you explained how the volunteers were sent, what you said was true. They would come to the party headquarters, then they would go to Bubanj Potok, to the barracks, and from there to the front. But the following is very important. Was there a frequent fluctuation of volunteers? For example, in one shift a man would leave as a volunteer of the Serbian Radical Party, he would remain at the front for two or three months, he would come home, and then he would go to the front-line again, but he would join Arkan's men or the White Eagles or the Serbian Guard, and so on? Did this fluctuation exist?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, to the best of my knowledge, yes. I have to say that in the park opposite the party, where Seselj saw them off, he didn't try to persuade them to commit crimes, to kill, to slaughter. No. He said, "Go and protect those people there." And I think it's important to mention that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you attend any of my speeches when I was seeing them off, when I told them how a volunteer of the Serbian Radical Party should behave on the battlefield?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it transpires --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That he must behave in a chivalrous manner, that he must be fearless, but that he must treat, in a noble and humane manner, children, women, and so on and so forth? Did I say those things?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I confirm that that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did we, as a party, condemn severely all war crimes, including looting, especially looting committed by others in the war-affected areas?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very often. You criticised that very often. Very often, that would happen when we heard that someone had committed a crime on the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And do you remember my fierce attacks on Arkan and Arkan's men, on Pantava [phoen] Guards, Mouseva's [phoen] Guard, the Serbian Guard, the White Eagles and so on?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I'm surprised by one thing. In this statement the Prosecution ascribes to you, you say the soldiers of the JNA were the most disciplined soldiers, that Arkan's men were very disciplined, and that the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party were not disciplined, that they were of poor quality. Did you really say that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I clarified this yesterday, but let me clarify once more. When I say "of poor quality," I don't mean that they were bad material, but these were people who are not trained. They were not trained professional soldiers and officers. In the nature of things, they should have gone through training and not been put in leadership positions. Well, let's not go into what I did or didn't say, but I think that ordinary people should not be pushed into positions alongside professional soldiers or men with military training, coming from the police and so on and so forth, and sent to lead military operations, because they don't know the rules of service, they don't know the conventions on the protection of prisoners of war, and so on and so forth. There are many things that the Prosecution and others are pressuring me to say about this statement, but I explained quite clearly, and today with a clear conscience I still say that I did not make the statement to the so-called investigators under oath and that it was not my statement that made the Prosecution draw up the indictment against you. My statement came later, after the indictment, so I did not say anything that might have consequences for them or for you. And I was never shown what I said, because I would have said, "Wait a minute, I didn't say that," because a man can make a mistake. But someone shouldn't be made to pay for that with his freedom or to suffer for that reason or to waste money on false statements. If I had been given a single statement of mine by the Tribunal or by the Prosecution, I would have objected and said, "Wait a minute, I didn't say it like this. You didn't translate this properly, you didn't formulate it properly," and our job today would have been much easier, and the Chamber and the Presiding Judge would have had an easier job. So would the Prosecutor and so would you, as the accused. And I also, but I was never given that statement of mine to look at, and to this day I don't know what it says there. And I'm afraid now what else I will hear read out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we get your point, but there's still something that is not clear to me. Yesterday, we saw a signature on a page where it was stated that the statement had been read back to you in your language, and at the bottom of this we saw your signature. And you confirmed that it was, indeed, your signature. Are you telling us today that you signed a document that was not telling the truth, you signed a false statement; is that what you are trying to tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Judge, I'll explain this to you. Yesterday and today, I say that the translation was never read out to me in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please respond by "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The statement was never read to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You provided enough explanation yesterday. When you signed this acknowledgement, where you state that the statement had been read back to you and so on and so forth, you put your signature at the bottom of something that was not telling the truth, because you signed this? You signed this statement, where you said it was your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I said what it says there. Well, yes, it's my signature, but the signature was always put on the document in English and it was never translated to me. Are you satisfied with my reply now, because that's the truth, and the only truth, and the real truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you only have a few minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stefanovic, do you know of a single instance where volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party participated in looting in war-affected areas and brought war booty to Serbia in an organised manner? Do you know of a single instance of that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of a single instance. Had they done this, by any chance, they would have been punished or branded in public by the leadership of the party. That was the standpoint of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And we expelled quite a few people from the Serbian Radical Party for lack of discipline, do you remember, because of individual instances of theft, failure to obey orders, and so on?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember that I was the only person in Serbia who dared to attack Arkan publicly, openly, looking him in the eye, because Arkan was all-powerful in Serbia? Was he omnipotent in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did whatever he wanted, and I remember that TV debate very well, when you told him some things, and later on I heard in person from the cameraman and the person hosting the show that they were terrified that he would take out a pistol and shoot you then and there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware that after all those attacks of mine, that Arkan sued me?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, when you told him that he had worn more socks on his head than you had worn on your foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I think that you came to the Palace of Justice at the time to attend the trial, when I turned up in the courtroom, and the judge said 15 minutes before the start of the trial Arkan's lawyer arrived, Toma Fila, and he withdrew the lawsuit against me; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So they didn't dare face me in court either; is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stefanovic, you must be aware that Ljubisa Savic, Mauser, the commander of the Kadarda Pantovi [phoen] paramilitary unit, was the deputy prime minister under Djindjic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of the Democratic Party for Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And also in Serbia, and the president of the party branch in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The party wasn't active all over Bosnia-Herzegovina, but only Republika Srpska; am I right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Initially, it was Bosnia-Herzegovina. Mauser was the president of the Democratic Party for Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992. But you are talking about the time when Republika Srpska already existed, and that was after 1995. But the answer is "yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware that The Hague Prosecution, in its indictment, accused me of crimes committed by Ljubisa Savic, Mauser, through my alleged participation in a joint criminal enterprise; are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm surprised at this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, from this, it follows that I was in a JCE with Zoran Djindjic, because instead of accusing Zoran Djindjic for what Ljubisa Savic, Mauser, did, they put this in the indictment against me. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, I know that Ljubisa, Mauser, established some sort of camp, and we had to intervene. Someone intervened to have this broken up, dissolved, in Bijeljina, and when the conflict broke out, he had already made false steps, and we had nothing in common with Mauser or any kind of military cooperation on anything else, to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that it was the president of the Serbian Chetnik Movement and later the president of the Serbian Radical Party, for Semberija, Mirko Blagojevic, on several occasions publicly opposed to Mauser's persecution of the Muslim population from Semberija, even the Muslims that belonged to the Serb Army?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is something I'm very familiar with, that that's precisely how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, we won't dwell there, because The Hague Prosecutor has all the documents -- those documents in its possession, all the statements made by Mirko Blagojevic in Bijeljina, when he stood up in defence of the local Muslim population. Now, do you know, for example, that even today, in the Serbian Radical Party in Bijeljina, we have quite a number of Muslims, even from "baj" [phoen] families, high-born families, and do you know that among the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party, there were Serb Catholics, so-called Croats, that we had Muslims, that we had Hungarians, that we even had Albanians?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember a case -- the case of a Hungarian who was a volunteer of the Serbian Radical Party, who was killed on the front, and the Roman Catholic priest in Vojvodina did not want to conduct a service at his burial because he was a member of the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that as for the Chetnik vojvoda, I proclaimed an Albanian a Chetnik vojvoda, in fact? His name was Mujo Bunjaku, and he had a new name, Oliver Dennis Barrett?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember that I promoted him to Chetnik vojvoda for bravery -- his bravery during the war?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that he was later killed in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know why he was killed? Let me remind you. He was killed by Vaso Djukanovic and Jozo Vujicic because he set up -- he lived together with the wife of Vaso Djukanovic, cohabited with her?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, do you know that The Hague -- the OTP of The Hague procured certain statements from witnesses who falsely accused me of having killed Dennis Barrett, that there are people who are ready to do things like that, too? You find that funny?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not funny; strange.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I find it funny, too, but I have to confront ludicrous accusations of that kind. Do you want to say something, Mr. Stefanovic? If not, we can move on. Now, you contacted -- you sent a letter, in fact, to the Prosecution on the 15th of May of this year, and in that letter, well, you say information for the Tribunal, and especially for the Trial Chamber, to the attention of the Trial Chamber in the Seselj trial, where you ask them to strike you from the list of Prosecution witnesses; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. At that time, you stipulated that you were promised that you would not have to appear as a witness live in this trial and that you certainly wouldn't be travelling to The Hague, and that Zoran Djindjic suggested that you should not accuse me falsely of crimes but that you should try and discredit me as a political adversary. And that is in paragraph 2 of that letter of yours that I was disclosed -- that was disclosed to me by the Prosecution. And you also state that when you gave the statement, that there was a man sitting in the room throughout, and that nobody told you who that man was and why he was in the room where you were making your statement, and that he was wearing a camouflage uniform; that he was white, of short build, very nervous, and rigid in his conduct. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember that man in uniform?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Can you -- were you able to recognise the uniform, whose army it belonged to?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't actually a camouflage uniform. It was -- well, I don't know. It was sort of dark green or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You say in your letter that the man left a negative effect on you, and that he made you nervous and that you -- and made you afraid, and you wanted to get away from him and leave the room because you felt insecure and afraid?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was sitting behind me, and I had the feeling that he was some sort of security detail and that people from the Prosecution team might have been afraid that I might not attack them physically, so I had the impression that he was in the room because of that. And I asked him, "What are you doing here, who are you?" And I even had a brief conversation and said that nobody introduced him to me, nor did anybody tell me who he was and what he was doing there. So I don't know anything about that person, about that man.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In your letter, you say that The Hague OTP never told you in what capacity they were interviewing you, but that they did not allow your lawyer to attend the interview; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, and they won't -- wouldn't allow my lawyer to attend my examination yesterday either, nor was my counsel allowed to attend at any time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Whereas according to the Serbian legal system, you have the right to a lawyer, whoever is examining or interviewing you; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and not only in the Serb system but in others too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And when a municipal service calls you up, you have the right to go there with a lawyer, accompanied by a lawyer, let alone when it's a court prosecutor or the police?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you told them at the time that you confirmed that you signed the statements, but that you never saw what it actually said in those statements; that's what you state in the letter?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I asked them to send me the statements. That's what I asked them to do there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone is not working again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you have one last question, could the court deputy make sure that a technician comes. It should have been done, well, a long time ago. Madam Registrar, do make sure that an engineer can come in. I can't work in these conditions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems to be working now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your time is up. You may have one last question, Mr. Seselj. Put it straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: As you state here, and that is in paragraph 3 on page 2, that your testimony was, in fact, made under duress because you weren't able to refuse Zoran Djindjic's request, now, did The Hague Tribunal ask you to have a meeting and discuss the letter with you, and then to show you the statement so that you could go through your statement to see what you actually said and what you didn't say and all the rest of it, because I'm rather surprised and astonished that they never showed you the statement. They must have had a proofing session with you before your testimony, and during that proofing session they must have shown you -- they ought to have shown you the statement and gone through the statement and informed if you made any corrections to that statement. So did any of that happen?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you for the third time that none of that happened, and that that's why I wrote a letter to the Tribunal, and that is a document. I'm sure there were other documents. I sent two or three documents requesting the Prosecution, or the Tribunal, or whoever, to provide me with the statements so that I could look through them and state my views. And I also asked them to -- well, I don't know -- to strike me from the list of witnesses, because my statement cannot be relevant. And I wrote that, too.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That completes my cross-examination. Thank you, Mr. Stefanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have any redirect, Ms. Dahl?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Yes, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Mr. Stefanovic, you said earlier today in your testimony that you looked at today's newspaper, the 'Glas Javnosti'?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your interview is in that paper today; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Do you recall the instructions at the end of your testimony yesterday from the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall the instructions I was given. But what have instructions got to do with it, with your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: You were instructed to refrain from any contact with the media; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I didn't contact the media. I gave the interview the day before yesterday. And let me tell you again the time and place and journalist. I gave an interview the day before yesterday. The journalist's name was Milosevic, the 'Glas Javnosti' journalist. We were sitting in the Atos Pizzeria in Belgrade where I'm a frequent guest. And we sat there from half past 3.00 until 5.00, and she recorded it all into a Dictaphone and then she went to the editorial offices and she could have released it the same day or the next day or two days later. That's up to the editorial board. But, anyway, I was very angry because the interview was -- did not come out yesterday. But what you're trying to do now has nothing to do with that, because I didn't come into contact -- I didn't contact the journalist. I left here at about 7.30, waited for half an hour for my transportation, which means that I was in town about 8.30. So it was impossible to give an interview after that. That would have been 9.30 and so on, because the papers go to the press at 8.00. So there's no need for you to try and do that. The fact that it came out today, that's got nothing to do with me. I'm not a member of the editorial board. It's up to the editors when they decide to publish it, and I've just told you when I gave the interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: You've answered my question. You said in your testimony earlier today that you analysed the signatures on your statement, and I'm quoting from the transcript: "They're not my signatures. They were scanned and only copied onto the Serbian language, because when I was signing, there was no translation into Serbian." Do you remember giving that testimony?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said something very similar to what you've just stated. I never signed the Serbian version. That's it, there you have it, never. If there's a signature there, then it's a forgery. I only signed the English version, which wasn't translated to me, nor was it read back to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: And let me make sure we're talking about the same documents. I'm referring to the 2006 statement in the Serbian language. Is that the one you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I challenge that this was my authentic statement, because as far as I was able to see, many of the -- well, I don't have the integral statement, I don't have the whole of it. I don't know what it says in this statement, either. All I read here with my very own eyes is that it was 0602436, paragraphs 21 and 26, and I stated my views about that yesterday and today. So they are totally untrue, and I say with full responsibility that I never said any of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: For the Chamber's convenience, I have obtained from the evidence vault at the Tribunal the original signed copies bearing Mr. Stefanovic's original signature in blue ink on both the English and Serbian versions, and I'd like to tender them into evidence to supplement the copies that you received and marked for identification yesterday. The ERN number on the top of the Serbian language document is 0601-2431, and it ends at 0601-2455. The English original --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I see the documents in Serbian, because we didn't have them before.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: For the record, the English signed original bears ERN range 0601-2396 and concludes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have here in front of me your statement in Serbian. I also have in front of me your signature in blue ink. What do you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I really can't remember what it says here. Well, I don't know all that it says there. I never read it all, and I say that with full responsibility, that I never read that document. And I don't know what the document -- what it says in the document. So why didn't you provide me with that document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask for the first page to be put on the ELMO. Can it be put on the ELMO, Madam Registrar, so that the first page can be seen and shown to the witness in his language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no need to put that on the overhead projector. I don't deny that it's my signature. But what I'm telling you is this: Why wasn't I provided with the statement, when I requested in writing that the Prosecution provide me with it? And I'm telling you that I never read it, and many of the things that are written in there are not what -- are things I did not say. I say that under oath. So there's no need to put it on the overhead projector. That is my signature. It couldn't have been signed by anyone else but me, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You admit that you signed the text in your own language and the text in English. You signed both versions. Well, we have here material evidence of it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember what I signed. All I remember is that I signed everything, but that nobody told me what it says in those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, give us a number for the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But each and every page was signed, not just the first one, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An MFI number, please, because we shall determine the final admission later on.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P656 marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, to complete the record, the last page of the English language statement, signed by the witness, was 0601-2430. It is the same document translated into English as the original Serbian that I have tendered. If the Chamber would like to see this, which also has the original signature of the witness, I'm at your convenience or I can put it back in the vault.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But with regard to the English version, we already had it. But we shall check the original. Yes, we can see the signature in blue ink. Good, you can put it back into the vault. Do you have other questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Mr. Stefanovic, you've just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: You've just told the Chamber that you were never given a copy of your statements to review in advance of your testimony. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Do you deny that we had an appointment for last Friday in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The answer was yes, the interpreter didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: So we did not have an appointment; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have a meeting, but I asked for that in May.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I offered to provide you with a full set of your statements this past Friday in Belgrade, didn't I?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, but you could have given it to me on Saturday. I couldn't have gone on Friday, which was a saints day, so I couldn't have done that on the Friday.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: After I travelled to Belgrade to meet with you, you didn't show up for the appointment?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was absent for justified reasons.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: You didn't call me to tell me you weren't coming?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: And I told you the Registry officer would be bringing a full set of your statements for you in preparation for the videolink, didn't I?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. I don't understand. What is it you just said?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: The Registry has a full set of your statements there with you for your testimony right now; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: You met with the Prosecution investigators in February 2003?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But nobody showed me these documents here.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Mr. Stefanovic, you met with the Prosecution investigators in February 2003; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: And you signed a statement dated 12 February 2003?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: That's the same statement we talked about in court yesterday and today?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Judges, on that statement, I have an objection. Mr. Stefanovic, you'll have to keep quiet while I present my objection. On this statement dated 2003, there is no signature of Mr. Stefanovic's in the Serbian version. However, at the bottom of the page, it always says "signed." But I assume that applies to the English version, not the Serbian version. In the 2003 Serbian version, Mr. Stefanovic's signature is not there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no need to say that. We knew that already. Please continue, Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Mr. Stefanovic, you remained in contact with the Prosecution the following year, 2004?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, probably. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: You remained in contact with the Prosecution throughout 2005?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: You had a meeting with a Prosecution investigator in the beginning of 2006, in February, at the field office; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: You reported that you had some safety concerns?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: You said you were willing to testify before this Tribunal, but you wanted protection?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: You told the investigator that Mr. Petkovic was negotiating to become a witness for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: You told the investigator that a bodyguard of Mr. Seselj's was trying to contact you, and you perceived that to be a threat?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which bodyguard. I was in contact with him, not Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Mr. Panic.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Panic? Well, I was in contact with him. Why would I be afraid of him? He was in conflict with Seselj, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: You told the investigator, when you met on 19 February 2007, that Mr. Panic was trying to contact you over the phone?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the investigator wrote, but I always talked to Mr. Panic, who was not on good terms with Seselj, so I don't know where the problem is. Why would I be afraid of him?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Mr. President, I didn't intervene straight away because I was inquisitive and interested to know what the answer would be of Mr. Stefanovic to -- what his response to the Prosecutor would be, but these were impermissibly leading questions, and you never ruled that Mr. Stefanovic should be proclaimed a hostile witness vis a vis the Prosecution, which would allow Madam Dahl to put leading questions. These are all leading questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question is not whether the questions are leading or not. We just need to know why he asked to be protected and why he no longer requests protective measures. That's the mystery.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Mr. Stefanovic, can you answer my question, please? You told the investigator that Mr. Panic was trying to contact you; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDER STEFANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't tell the investigator that. It was impossible that I was afraid of Panic then, now, or any time, since Panic is in conflict with Seselj since 2000 or 2001, so there's no reason why I should be afraid of Panic. So that means that that's not true. And the second key point, the question raised by the Judge, I'll respond to that, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
